segments.text: A man on a ladder was unscrewing my father's name from the hardware store.
That sign had hung over Main Street for 41 years.
I studied the ladder while my husband laughed and called it the best joke of his life.
By his truck, a man in a gray suit checked his watch and muttered,
Friday, every winter morning, my husband had scraped my windshield before I woke.
Now he stood on the sidewalk in his good shirt, rocking on his heels like a man waiting for a parade through the window.
The old man at the register rang up a can of paint in his church tie.
The brass letters came off one at a time.
The brick behind them was a brighter red than the rest of the wall.
Down the block, the barber stopped sweeping to watch.
The man in the gray suit handed my husband a folder.
10 o'clock tomorrow, Brent, he said, title office.
Bring your wife. Brent kissed the top of my head. I led him.
My father opened that store before I was born and put me on the key machine at 12.
Cut one. Test one, he used to say. He died two winters ago.
And the building came to me. Brent called it dead weight.
Every Sunday over breakfast, he gave the same speech.
Sell it, Dana. Even house has the places dying.
I said no every time. How had worked the floor since before I could reach the counter.
And the others had been there nearly as long.
Then one Sunday in March, Brent sat down as four.
You're right, he said. I'm sorry. He never raised the store again.
That same Thursday before the ladder came.
Hell found me in the stockroom with one hand resting on the folded dollar in his shirt pocket.
He told the staff, the signs going to the painter, he said.
He told the sign men, it's going to the dumpster.
I went back out front and waited for the ladder.
12 days earlier, on a morning Brent had already scraped my windshield clear.
I opened his glove box for a tire gauge.
Under it sat a purchase agreement from my father's building, $640,000 closing Friday at 10.
My name was signed across the bottom. In handwriting, that was almost mine.
Behind it was a receipt for $50,000 of earnest money signed for by Brent as my agent.
Non-refundable, it said.
And the buyer's remedy ran against the seller.
That was me. The money had already gone to a marina in Florida.
Staple to the back, a site plan showed a drive through pharmacy where my father's key machines did.
I read every page standing in the driveway.
Then I put them back exactly as I'd found them.
My lawyer laid it out at her kitchen table.
If I refused Friday, the buyer would sue the only maim on the contract.
If I signed, the pharmacy would rise on my father's floor.
She slid a third option across the table and told me what it would cost.
I asked the person I trusted most for a favor.
He said, yes, before I finished asking.
That was why I studied the ladder on Thursday.
A man who believes he has won stops checking the paperwork.
The county office closed at five.
The clerk had stamped my father's permits for most of my life.
I held the pen over the last line until she cleared her throat.
After this line, no one who shared my father's name would ever own that wall again.
Then I signed. The stamp came down at $4.58.
Nobody on earth could take it back.
Friday at 10, the title office had a bowl of mints and a long oak table.
Brent sat in the middle chair pen on cap grinning at the papers.
The man in the gray suit set across from him.
Yellow tabs marked every line Brent expected me to sign.
I took the chair at the end.
The title agent opened her laptop to confirm the parcel before anyone signed.
She stopped typing.
Mr. Brent, she said, the county shows this property transferred yesterday at $4.58.
$1 to the people who work at 4.
In the doorway, house stood in his church tie with one hand flat over an empty shirt pocket.
Tell me this is a joke, Brent said.
Nobody laughed.
His grin held one breath after the rest of his face let go.
The man in the gray suit slid a demand across the table.
$50,000 due in 10 days.
